items.prompt: What is the scientific name for the group of bones that forms the framework of the body?

options.label: The cartilage
options.feedback: Cartilage is a separate, flexible tissue that covers bone ends inside joints, not the overall bone framework.

options.label: The skeleton
options.feedback: Correct — the skeleton is the complete set of bones that supports the body and gives it its shape.

options.label: The marrows
options.feedback: Marrow is the soft inner material inside many bones, not the name for the whole bone framework.

options.label: The tendons
options.feedback: Tendons are the cords that attach muscle to bone, not the bone framework itself.

items.ok_line: The skeleton is the whole set of bones.
items.ko_line: Cartilage, marrow, and tendons are parts, not the whole frame.
items.exp_text: The skeleton is the complete framework of bones in the body. It supports the body, protects organs, and gives the body its shape.

items.prompt: How many separate bones make up an adult human skeleton?

options.label: About 50
options.feedback: That is far too few; even a child's skull alone has more than a dozen bones.

options.label: Exactly 100
options.feedback: An adult has more than a hundred bones; many small bones in the hands and feet add up.

options.label: Approximately 300
options.feedback: A newborn has more than 300 bones, but many fuse together as the person grows, leaving about 206 in an adult.

options.label: About 206
options.feedback: Correct — an adult skeleton has roughly 206 bones; some babies are born with a few extra small ones that later fuse.

items.exp_text: An adult human skeleton contains about 206 bones. A newborn has more, but some bones fuse together during growth, reducing the total.

items.prompt: What is the name of the long bone in the upper arm, between the shoulder and the elbow?

options.label: The humerus
options.feedback: Correct — the humerus is the single long bone of the upper arm.

options.label: The femur
options.feedback: The femur is the thigh bone in the leg, not the upper arm.

options.label: The radius
options.feedback: The radius is one of the two bones in the forearm, on the thumb side.

options.label: The tibia
options.feedback: The tibia is the shin bone in the lower leg, not in the arm.

items.ok_line: The humerus runs from shoulder to elbow.
items.ko_line: Femur, radius, and tibia are bones of the leg or forearm.
items.exp_text: The humerus is the long bone of the upper arm. It connects at the shoulder and at the elbow, and it is the largest bone in the arm.

items.prompt: What is the name of the flat bone at the front of the chest, to which the ribs attach?

options.label: The clavicle
options.feedback: The clavicle is the collarbone, which lies above the ribs and does not attach to them directly.

options.label: The scapula
options.feedback: The scapula is the shoulder blade at the back, not the bone at the front of the chest.

options.label: The sternum
options.feedback: Correct — the sternum, also called the breastbone, is the flat bone in the middle of the chest where ribs meet.

options.label: The vertebra
options.feedback: A vertebra is one of the bones of the spine, not the front chest bone.

items.ok_line: The sternum is the flat front chest bone.
items.ko_line: Clavicle, scapula, and vertebrae are different bones.
items.exp_text: The sternum is the flat bone at the front center of the chest. Most ribs connect to it, helping form the rib cage.

items.prompt: What is the name of the bones that make up the spine?

options.label: Ribs
options.feedback: Ribs are the curved bones of the chest, not part of the spine.

options.label: Pelvis
options.feedback: The pelvis is the large bone ring at the base of the trunk, not the spine itself.

options.label: Cranium
options.feedback: The cranium is the part of the skull that encloses the brain, not the spine.

options.label: Vertebrae
options.feedback: Correct — the spine is made of a stack of bones called vertebrae.

items.ok_line: Each individual spine bone is a vertebra.
items.ko_line: Ribs, pelvis, and cranium are not spine bones.
items.exp_text: The spine is made of many small bones stacked one on top of another, and each of these bones is called a vertebra. Together they form the vertebral column.

items.prompt: What is the largest bone in the human body?

options.label: The humerus
options.feedback: The humerus is the upper arm bone, but it is shorter and thinner than the thigh bone.

options.label: The femur
options.feedback: Correct — the femur, the thigh bone, is the longest and heaviest bone in the body.

options.label: The tibia
options.feedback: The tibia is a lower leg bone and is smaller than the femur above it.

options.label: The pelvis
options.feedback: The pelvis is a large bone, but it is not a single long bone and is not the largest.

items.ok_line: The femur is the body's biggest bone.
items.ko_line: Humerus, tibia, and pelvis are all smaller than the femur.
items.exp_text: The femur, located in the thigh, is the longest and heaviest bone in the human body. It supports the body's weight when standing and walking.

items.prompt: What is the name of the dome-shaped bone that forms the top and sides of the head?

options.label: The jaw
options.feedback: The jaw is the lower bone of the mouth, not the dome of the head.

options.label: The spine
options.feedback: The spine runs down the back, not around the head.

options.label: The cranium
options.feedback: Correct — the cranium is the curved part of the skull that protects the brain.

options.label: The cheekbone
options.feedback: The cheekbone is a small bone of the face, not the whole upper skull.

items.ko_line: Jaw, spine, and cheekbone are not the skull's dome.
items.exp_text: The cranium is the rounded upper part of the skull. It is made of several bones fused together, forming a hard dome that encloses and protects the brain.

items.prompt: What is the name of the small bones that make up the fingers and toes?

options.label: Phalanges
options.feedback: Correct — the bones in the fingers and toes are called phalanges.

options.label: Metacarpals
options.feedback: Metacarpals are the bones of the palm of the hand, not the fingers themselves.

options.label: Tarsals
options.feedback: Tarsals are the bones of the ankle and back of the foot, not the toes.

options.label: Carpals
options.feedback: Carpals are the small bones of the wrist, not the fingers.

items.ok_line: Phalanges are the bones in fingers and toes.
items.ko_line: Metacarpals, tarsals, and carpals are different bone groups.
items.exp_text: Phalanges are the small bones that form the fingers and toes. Each finger except the thumb has three, and the thumb and each toe have two.

items.prompt: Which part of the skeleton protects the brain?

options.label: The rib cage
options.feedback: The rib cage protects the heart and lungs, not the brain.

options.label: The pelvis
options.feedback: The pelvis protects organs in the lower belly, not the brain.

options.label: The spine
options.feedback: The spine protects the spinal cord, not the brain itself.

options.label: The skull
options.feedback: Correct — the skull, especially the cranium, forms a hard shell around the brain.

items.ok_line: The skull is the brain's protective case.
items.ko_line: Rib cage, pelvis, and spine protect other structures.
items.exp_text: The skull is the bony structure of the head. Its cranium part completely surrounds the brain, shielding it from blows and impacts.

items.prompt: What type of joint is the elbow?

options.label: Ball-and-socket joint
options.feedback: A ball-and-socket joint, like the shoulder or hip, allows movement in many directions; the elbow does not.

options.label: Hinge joint
options.feedback: Correct — the elbow works like a hinge, allowing bending and straightening in one direction.

options.label: Pivot joint
options.feedback: A pivot joint, like between the top two neck vertebrae, allows rotation, not the elbow's bending.

options.label: Gliding joint
options.feedback: A gliding joint, like between wrist bones, allows bones to slide over each other, not hinge-like bending.

items.ok_line: The elbow bends like a door hinge.
items.ko_line: Ball-and-socket, pivot, and gliding joints move differently.
items.exp_text: The elbow is a hinge joint, meaning it opens and closes in a single plane, like a door hinge. This allows the arm to bend and straighten, but not to rotate sideways.
